extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature/poetics, dramatists and critics studying Aristotle's theory of poetry and drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging poetry, tragedy, comedy, and epic according to Aristotle's Poetics (definitions, parts, and priorities such as plot, character, diction, thought, song, scenery, unity, and catharsis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three differences distinguishing imitation (medium, objects, manner)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitative arts differ in (1) the medium (e.g., rhythm, tune, and metre; some arts use some of these means and not others), (2) the objects (men in action represented as better, worse, or as they are), and (3) the manner (by narration or by presenting the characters acting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: flute and lyre employ harmony and rhythm; dancing uses rhythm alone; there are arts that imitate by language alone (prose or verse). The poet may narrate (speaking in another personality or his own) or present characters living and moving before us. These three axes together determine kinds of imitation (e.g., epic, tragedy, comedy, dithyrambic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament (rhythm, harmony, song); in the form of action, not of narrative; and by arousing pity and fear effects the proper purgation (catharsis) of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language may be rendered sometimes in verse alone and sometimes with the aid of song; scenic equipment, song, and diction are all parts of tragedy. The end (the action) and its emotional effect (pity and fear → catharsis) are central to judging tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy must have six parts: Plot, Character, Diction, Thought, Scenery, and Song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These parts determine quality: two parts constitute the medium of imitation, one the manner, three the objects. All plays contain scenic accessories as well as Character, Plot, Diction, Song, and Thought. Relative importance of these parts is discussed elsewhere (plot most important, then character, then thought, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot (plot as the soul of tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot (the arrangement of incidents—the imitation of the action) is the first principle and the soul of a tragedy; incidents and their artistic arrangement are the end of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without action (plot) there cannot be a tragedy; there may be a tragedy without well-rendered character. Important tragic elements such as Reversal (peripeteia) and Recognition (anagnorisis) are parts of the plot and are primary sources of emotional interest. Novices tend to reach diction and portraiture before they can construct a proper plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity, completeness, and magnitude of action
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic action must be serious, complete (having a beginning, middle, and end), and of a certain magnitude; traditionally tragedy aims to confine action to a single revolution of the sun (unity of time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic differs by admitting broader chronological scope and no time-limits. The unity and completeness of the plot are essential criteria for evaluating whether an action qualifies as a proper tragic subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character's role and how it should be shown
rubrics_metrics.description: Character (ethos) is that in virtue of which we ascribe certain qualities to agents; it reveals moral purpose (what a person chooses or avoids) and is the second-most important element after plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character is subsidiary to action—actions determine happiness or the contrary. Speeches must make moral purpose manifest by showing choices; mere well-finished speeches expressive of character are not sufficient without a coherent plot. Painting analogy: Polygnotus delineates character well; Zeuxis excels in other qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia) as a component
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent in given circumstances—where a statement is proved or a general truth enunciated—and ranks third in importance among elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In oratory thought corresponds to political art and rhetoric. Thought appears where something is demonstrated or where general maxims are spoken; it contributes to the intellectual content of speeches and the play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (lexis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the expression of meaning in words; its essence is the same in verse and prose and includes the mere metrical arrangement of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction is distinct from Song (musical element). Careful choice and arrangement of words (including metre) affect the artistic quality; diction can be perfected before plot-construction in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song (melos) as an embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Song is the chief of the embellishments (musical element) and is one of the constituent parts of tragedy employed in certain parts of the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Song contributes strongly to emotional effect and is part of the medium (language embellished with rhythm, harmony, and song). It is more artistic than scenery but subordinate to plot, character, and thought in ordering importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenery and scenic equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenery (spectacle) is a component of tragedy and has an emotional attraction of its own, but is the least artistic part and the least connected with the poetic art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The power of tragedy is felt even apart from representation and actors; scenic effects influence emotion but do not substitute for well-constructed plot, character, diction, or thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation: narration vs representation
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may imitate either by narration (speaking in another personality or his own, unchanged) or by presenting characters as living and moving (dramatic representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This difference affects genre distinctions (e.g., epic is narrative, drama is representational). From one perspective poets like Sophocles and Homer may be similar (they both imitate higher types), while from another perspective Sophocles and Aristophanes share the dramatic mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of types (better, worse, as they are)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation must represent men either as better than they are, worse than they are, or as they are; moral differences (goodness and badness) distinguish types and genres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homer makes men better than they are (noble); Cleophon depicts them as they are; comic/parodic writers depict them worse. Tragedy tends to portray men better than in real life; Comedy aims at representing men as worse (ludicrous). Painting analogies (Polygnotus, Pauson, Dionysius) illustrate this point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of rhythm, tune, and metre in medium distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Different arts employ combinations of rhythm, tune, and metre: some (flute, lyre) use harmony and rhythm; dancing uses rhythm alone; some poetic forms combine all three (dithyrambic, nomic poetry, tragedy, comedy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence or absence of these elements defines the medium and hence the kind of imitation; e.g., dancing imitates character and action by rhythmical movement without harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and nature of Comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is an imitation of characters of a lower type; the ludicrous is a subdivision of the ugly and consists in some defect or ugliness which is not painful or destructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the comic mask is ugly/distorted but not painful. Comedy historically took shape later; the comic plot origin and technical devices are noted but the definitional criterion is the representation of the low or ludicrous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between Epic and Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry imitates noble action in verse (hexameter), is narrative in form, admits only one kind of metre, and has no strict limits of time; Tragedy is dramatic action-focused and typically confines itself to a single day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All elements of an epic poem are found in tragedy, but not all elements of tragedy are found in epic. The time-limit (unity of time) and the form (narrative vs action) are key distinguishing criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powerful plot devices: Reversal and Recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal (peripeteia) and Recognition (anagnorisis) are among the most powerful elements of emotional interest in tragedy and are parts of the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices contribute strongly to pity and fear and hence to catharsis. They are structural plot elements to be arranged artfully in the incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins of poetry: imitation and rhythm/harmony instincts
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry arises from two deep human instincts: (1) the instinct of imitation (present from childhood) and (2) the instinct for harmony and rhythm; pleasure in imitation and learning underlies poetic creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This anthropological observation grounds why humans take pleasure in likenesses and why metre/rhythm developed; it informs why certain media and forms appeal and how poetic talent develops into distinct genres.
